Dihedral linking invariants

Patricia Cahn Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Smith College, USA Email address: pcahn@smith.edu , Elise Catania Address: School of Mathematics, College of Science and Engineering, University of Minnesota, USA Email address: catan042@umn.edu , Sarangoo Chimgee Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Smith College, USA Email address: sara.chimgee@gmail.com , Olivia Del Guercio Address: Department of Mathematics, Rice University, USA Email address: od6@rice.edu and Jack Kendrick Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Washington, USA Email address: jackgk@uw.edu
Abstract.

A Fox p-colored knot KK in S3S^{3} gives rise to a corresponding pp-fold dihedral branched cover MM of S3S^{3} along KK. The pre-image of the knot KK under the covering map is a p+12\dfrac{p+1}{2}-component link LL in MM, and the set of pairwise linking numbers of the components of LL is an invariant of KK. This powerful invariant played a key role in the development of early knot tables, and appears in formulas for many other important knot and manifold invariants. We give an algorithm for computing this invariant for all odd pp, generalizing an algorithm of Perko. We then extend this algorithm to compute linking numbers of arbitrary curves in a pp-fold dihedral branched cover of S3S^{3} along KK. As an application, we compute Kjuchukova’s ribbon obstruction Ξp\Xi_{p} using a method of the first author and Kjuchukova. We also tabulate the dihedral linking invariant for all pp-colorings of prime knots of crossing number less than or equal to 13, with p≥3p\geq 3 prime. Finally, we demonstrate the strength of the dihedral linking invariant by comparing it to several polynomial invariants. For example, the dihedral linking invariant distinguishes more than 98% of the 1183 prime non-mutant knot pairs with the same Fox coloring invariant and the same HOMFLY-PT polynomial through 13 crossings.

1. Introduction

Linking numbers of curves in branched covers of the 3-sphere along a knot KK are a rich source of invariants of KK. One such invariant is the pp-dihedral linking invariant, which is defined for Fox pp-colorable knots, where pp is odd. A Fox pp-coloring of KK gives rise to a pp-fold branched covering f:M→S3f:M\rightarrow S^{3} along KK. The knot KK lifts to a (p+1)/2(p+1)/2-component link in MM, and the set of pairwise linking numbers of its components is the dihedral linking invariant of the pp-colored knot KK.

We refer the reader to  [24] for details on the rich history of non-cyclic branched covering spaces in knot theory and their associated linking invariants, particularly the key role they played in the development of early knot tables. For example, using computations of Bankwitz and Schumann [1], Reidemeister used the dihedral linking invariant to distinguish two knots with the same Alexander polynomial  [25].

Linking invariants derived from branched covers, and dihedral covers in particular, also appear in formulas for many other knot and manifold invariants, for example: Cappell and Shaneson’s formula for the Rokhlin μ\mu-invariant [10], Litherland’s formula for the Casson-Gordon invariants [19], and Kjuchukova’s Ξp\Xi_{p}-invariant  [16, 6], which gives an obstruction to a knot being homotopy-ribbon [4, 13], as well as bounds on 4-genera associated to a pp-colored knot  [5].

Perko gave an explicit geometric algorithm for computing the dihedral linking invariant for all 3-colorable knots in his 1964 thesis, and tabulated the invariant for all such knots up to 11 crossings  [22]. The primary challenge in generalizing Perko’s algorithm to p>3p>3 is to find a simple way to combinatorially encode a cell structure on the covering space, which also lends itself to fast computation. We develop such a method and give a fully general geometric algorithm for computing the dihedral linking invariant for all pp-colorable knots. We then tabulate the invariant for pp-colorable prime knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13. Code and additional data can be found at  [3].

Hartley and Murasugi gave general, algebraic formulas for linking numbers of branch curves via the Reidemeister-Schreier algorithm, contrasting them with Perko’s method in  [22], which they say requires “considerable geometric intuition”  [15]. Hartley used the method in [15] to show that many knots are non-invertible using linking numbers derived from other metacyclic covering spaces [14]; in that paper, he also discusses his implementation of the Hartley-Murasugi method. A number of additional methods have been introduced for computing the dihedral linking invariant for particular knots and knot families. For example, in  [23, Theorem 4], Perko gave an elegant method for computing linking numbers for 2-bridge knots from the Schubert normal form. Perko also introduced a visually appealing way of computing the linking invariant from a Perko surface, a Seifert-like surface constructed from the diagram of a pp-colored knot [24]; see Figure  1. However, such surfaces may not exist for a given diagram of the knot, and it is not known whether every colorable knot admits a diagram with a Perko surface.

We now review the necessary background information. Consider a diagram DKD_{K} of KK, and let pp be an odd number. A Fox pp-coloring of DKD_{K} is an assignment of the values {0,1,…,p−1}\{0,1,\dots,p-1\} to the arcs of DKD_{K} such that at each crossing, a+b≡2​cmodpa+b\equiv 2c\mod p, where aa and cc are the values on the understands and cc is the value on the overstrand. Equivalently, a Fox pp-coloring is described by a surjection ρ:π1​(S3−K)↠Dp\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K)\twoheadrightarrow D_{p}, where DpD_{p} denotes the dihedral group of order 2​p2p. Label the vertices of a regular pp-gon {0,…,p−1}\{0,\dots,p-1\}. Denote by Refn∈Dp\text{Ref}_{n}\in D_{p} the reflection over a line through the nt​hn^{th} vertex of a regular pp-gon, and denote by Refn​(x)∈{0,…,p−1}\text{Ref}_{n}(x)\in\{0,\dots,p-1\} the image of vertex xx under this reflection. The standard meridian of an arc in the diagram DKD_{K} colored nn is mapped to the reflection Refn\text{Ref}_{n}, and a crossing with overstrand colored cc and understrands colored aa and bb satisfies Refc​(a)=b.\text{Ref}_{c}(a)=b.

Given a pp-coloring ρ:π1​(S3−K)↠Dp\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K)\twoheadrightarrow D_{p}, the corresponding irregular pp-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3}, denoted MρM_{\rho}, is the branched cover of S3S^{3} along KK corresponding to a subgroup ρ−1​(ℤ2)\rho^{-1}(\mathbb{Z}_{2}) of π1​(S3−K)\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K). The knot KK has one lift K0⊂MρK^{0}\subset M_{\rho} of branching index 1, and (p−1)/2(p-1)/2 lifts K1,…,K(p−1)/2⊂MρK^{1},\dots,K^{(p-1)/2}\subset M_{\rho} of branching index 2.

The linking number lk​(α,β)∈ℚ\text{lk}(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{Q} of two knots α\alpha, β\beta in a closed, connected, oriented 3-manifold MM is defined whenever both α\alpha and β\beta are rationally null-homologous in MM. Suppose Σα\Sigma_{\alpha} is a 2-chain such that ∂Σα=k⋅α\partial\Sigma_{\alpha}=k\cdot\alpha, where k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}. Then lk​(α,β)=1k​(β⋅Σα)\text{lk}(\alpha,\beta)=\dfrac{1}{k}\left(\beta\cdot\Sigma_{\alpha}\right), where ⋅\cdot denotes the algebraic intersection number. This linking number is well-defined and symmetric  [2]. If either α\alpha or β\beta represent a nonzero class in H1​(M,ℚ),H_{1}(M;\mathbb{Q}), we set lk​(α,β)=∞\text{lk}(\alpha,\beta)=\infty. The pp-dihedral linking invariant of KK together with a choice of pp-coloring ρ\rho of KK is the multiset

D​L​N​(K,ρ)={lk​(Ki,Kj)|i≠j∈{0,1,…,(p−1)/2}}.DLN(K,\rho)=\left\{\text{lk}(K^{i},K^{j})|i\neq j\in\{0,1,\dots,(p-1)/2\}\right\}.

An outline of our algorithm is as follows. Neuwirth gave a combinatorial method for constructing a branched cover of a 3-manifold MM along a 1-subcomplex KK from a choice of splitting complex for KK, and a permutation representation of the knot group π1​(M−K)↠Sn\pi_{1}(M-K)\twoheadrightarrow S_{n} corresponding to the desired branched cover [21]. We carry out this construction where M=S3M=S^{3}, the splitting complex CC is the cone on KK, and the permutation representation is the coloring ρ:π1​(S3−K)↠Dp⩽Sp\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K)\twoheadrightarrow D_{p}\leqslant S_{p}. The resulting construction gives the irregular pp-fold cover MρM_{\rho} of S3S^{3} along KK, equipped with a cell structure determined by the lift C~\tilde{C} of CC to MρM_{\rho}. As noted in  [24], this cell structure on MM actually dates back to Wirtinger.

We then find a rational 2-chain Σj\Sigma^{j} bounding each connected component KjK^{j} of the singular set, by solving a q​n×q​nqn\times qn system of linear equations, where nn is the number of crossings in a chosen diagram of KK and q=p−12q=\dfrac{p-1}{2}. If a solution exists, we conclude KjK^{j} is rationally null-homologous, and lk​(Ki,Kj)\text{lk}(K^{i},K^{j}) exists provided KiK^{i} is rationally null-homologous as well. If no solution exists, KjK^{j} is not rationally null-homologous. To compute lk​(Ki,Kj)\text{lk}(K^{i},K^{j}) we choose a push-off of KiK^{i} transverse to the 2-chain Σj\Sigma^{j}, and compute the signed intersection number Ki⋅ΣjK^{i}\cdot\Sigma^{j}.

In Section  2, we carry out this algorithm for the Figure-8 knot. We then turn to computing the invariant for an arbitrary pp-colored knot (K,ρ)(K,\rho). In Section  3, we introduce configuration diagrams, a fully combinatorial method for encoding the cell structure on the corresponding branched cover MρM_{\rho}. In Section  4, we find a rational 2-chain Σj\Sigma^{j} with boundary KjK^{j} using the configuration diagram of (K,ρ)(K,\rho), and in Section  5, we compute the linking number of KjK^{j} and KiK^{i} using the configuration diagram of (K,ρ)(K,\rho). Additional worked examples are in Section  6.

In Section 7, we explain how to extend the algorithm above to compute linking numbers between lifts of curves γ,δ⊂S3−K\gamma,\delta\subset S^{3}-K to the pp-fold dihedral cover MρM_{\rho} corresponding to a pp-coloring ρ\rho of KK. We call such curves pseudo-branch curves. An algorithm for computing linking numbers of lifts of pseudo-branch curves was given by the first author and Kjuchukova in [7] in the case p=3p=3, for dihedral covers, and for all pp in [8] in the case of cyclic covers. Such linking numbers appear in a formula for Kjuchukova’s Ξp\Xi_{p} invariant [16], which is of interest because it gives rise to a homotopy ribbon obstruction [4], [13], and bounds on 4-genera associated to a pp-colorable knot [5]. The first author and Kjuchukova gave a diagrammatic algorithm for computing Ξp\Xi_{p} [6]. In part because the algorithm in  [7] for computing linking numbers of pseudo-branch curves was specific to the case p=3p=3, the examples in [6] are carried out only for p=3p=3. The above extension of the algorithm to the computation of linking numbers of pseudo-branch curves for arbitrary odd pp allows us to carry out the algorithm in [6] when p>3p>3. As an application, we carry out one such example in Section 7.3.

In Section 8, we give an overview of our methods for tabulating the dihedral linking invariant for prime knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 that are pp-colorable, for prime p≥3p\geq 3. The code used to produce the tabulation and the tabulation itself are available at  [3]. We then compare the dihedral linking invariant to the strength of the Fox coloring invariant alone (that is, the number of non-trivial pp-colorings of KK for each odd prime pp), as well as to the Alexander, Jones, HOMFLY-PT, Kauffman and Khovanov polynomials, using data tabulated in KnotInfo [20]; the Khovanov data on KnotInfo is computed using  [26]. The dihedral linking invariant proves to be particularly strong, especially when restricted to non-mutant knot pairs. For each given polynomial invariant above, the dihedral linking invariant distinguishes between 94.3% and 98.3% of non-mutant prime knot pairs of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 with the same Fox coloring invariant and the same given polynomial invariant.

2. Extended Example

In this section, let KK be the Figure-8 knot, with diagram DKD_{K} and 5-coloring ρ\rho as shown in Figure  2. We will carry out our algorithm on KK.

The 3-manifold MρM_{\rho} can be constructed combinatorially from the diagram DKD_{K} by means of a splitting complex for KK, namely the cone on DKD_{K} [21]. First, the cone on DKD_{K} gives rise to an associated cell structure on S3S^{3}, as shown in Figure  2, with cone point at infinity.

We label the cells as follows:

  1. (1)

    “horizontal” 1-cells k0k_{0}, k1k_{1}, k2k_{2}, k3k_{3}, which are arcs in the diagram DKD_{K} of KK;

  2. (2)

    “vertical” 1-cells a0a_{0}, a1a_{1}, a2a_{2}, a3a_{3}, below each crossing of DKD_{K};

  3. (3)

    “vertical” 2-cells A0A_{0}, A1A_{1}, A2A_{2}, A3A_{3}, below each arc of DKD_{K}

  4. (4)

    one 3-cell, EE, the complement of the cone

  5. (5)

    one 0-cell ee at the cone point

  6. (6)

    a 0-cell eie_{i} at the head of each arc kik_{i}

Denote the kk-skeleton of this cell structure by CkC^{k}.

Next we lift this cell structure to the dihedral cover MρM_{\rho} of S3S^{3}, branched along KK determined by the 5-coloring ρ\rho of KK shown in Figure  2. Consider the open cover of the 2-skeleton C2C^{2} which consists of: a small open 3-ball UiU_{i} centered at eie_{i} and containing a segment of the over-arc at crossing ii; a small tubular neighborhood VjV_{j} of each arc kik_{i} of DKD_{K} disjoint from DK−kiD_{K}-k_{i}, and a (topological) 3-ball neighborhood WW of ee disjoint from DKD_{K} and containing the remainder of the 2-skeleton S2S^{2}; see Figure  3. Together with the 3-cell EE, this forms an open cover of S3S^{3}. It suffices to understand the lift of the cell structure on its intersection with each of the UiU_{i}, VjV_{j}, WW, and EE.

Since MρM_{\rho} is a 5-fold dihedral cover of (S3,K)(S^{3},K), KK has one index-1 preimage K0K_{0} and two index-2 preimages K1K_{1} and K2K_{2}. Denote the three corresponding lifts of each 1-cell kik_{i} by ki0k_{i}^{0}, ki1k_{i}^{1}, and ki2k_{i}^{2}.

There are five lifts of the 3-cell EE, denoted E0​…​E4E^{0}\dots E^{4}. We label them as follows. Let aa and bb be two points in EE, and g:[0,1]→S3g:[0,1]\rightarrow S^{3} a path from aa to bb which intersects exactly one of the two-cells AiA_{i} once, transversely, where AiA_{i} is colored nn. Denote by g~m\tilde{g}_{m} the lift of gg such that g~m​(0)∈En\tilde{g}_{m}(0)\in E^{n}. Then g~m​(1)∈ERefn​(m)\tilde{g}_{m}(1)\in E^{\text{Ref}_{n}(m)}. This labelling is well-defined since the monodromy homomorphism ρ\rho is trivial on the complement EE of the cone.

The neighborhood WW of the 00-cell ee has 5 lifts to MM. The pair (W,C2)(W,C^{2}) is homeomorphic to the cone on (S2,GK)(S^{2},G_{K}) where GKG_{K} is the 4-valent graph corresponding to the knot diagram DKD_{K}. Its five lifts intersect the 3-cells EiE_{i} as shown in Figure  4. The subscripts on the EiE_{i} are labeled by the 5 Dehn colorings of KK corresponding to the Fox coloring ρ\rho, as defined in [12].

The other cells aia_{i} and AiA_{i} above each have 5 lifts to MρM_{\rho}. We introduce a systematic way of labelling these cells.

Since DKD_{K} has an even number of crossings, the vector field −∂/∂z-\partial/\partial z along KK has two lifts along each of the index-2 curves K1K_{1} and K2K_{2}. We choose one such lift V1V^{1} along K1K^{1} and one lift V2V^{2} along K2K^{2}. Now denote by Ri1R^{1}_{i} and Li1L^{1}_{i} the two lifts of AiA_{i} adjacent to ki1k_{i}^{1}, with V1V^{1} tangent to Ri1R^{1}_{i}. The five lifts of aia_{i} are bib_{i}, ri1r_{i}^{1}, li1l_{i}^{1}, ri2r_{i}^{2}, and li2l_{i}^{2}, as shown in Figure  5.

We can follow this process for each of the remaining crossings, generating three systems of eight inhomogeneous linear equations in eight variables, one system per 2-chain. We can then solve these systems of equations to determine values of each xijx^{j}_{i}, yijy_{i}^{j}, and zijz_{i}^{j} in the 2-chains. These values yield a 2-chain whose boundary is the relevant lift of the knot.

3. General Setup

Let KK be a knot and ρ:π1​(S3−K)↠Dp\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K)\twoheadrightarrow D_{p} a pp-coloring of KK. Let MρM_{\rho} denote the corresponding pp-fold irregular branched cover of (S3,K)(S^{3},K). Let DKD_{K} be a diagram of KK with an even number of crossings nn; we can always arrange this by adding a crossing with a first Reidemeister move.

As in Section  2, we consider a cell structure on S3S^{3} determined by the cone on DKD_{K}.

  1. (1)

    “horizontal” 1-cells k0k_{0}, k1k_{1}, …\dots, kn−1k_{n-1}, which are arcs in the diagram DKD_{K} of KK;

  2. (2)

    “vertical” 1-cells a0a_{0}, a1a_{1}, …\dots, an−1a_{n-1}, below each crossing of DKD_{K};

  3. (3)

    “vertical” 2-cells A0A_{0}, A1A_{1}, …\dots, An−1A_{n-1}, below each arc of DKD_{K}

  4. (4)

    one 3-cell, EE, the complement of the cone

  5. (5)

    one 0-cell ee at the cone point

  6. (6)

    one 0-cell eie_{i} at the head of each arc kik_{i}

Denote the kk-skeleton by CkC^{k}.

Next we lift this cell structure to the dihedral cover MρM_{\rho} of S3S^{3}, branched along KK determined by the pp-coloring ρ\rho of KK. We let UiU_{i} and ViV_{i} represent neighborhoods of crossing ii and arc kik_{i} as before; see Figure  3.

Since MρM_{\rho} is a pp-fold dihedral cover of (S3,K)(S^{3},K), KK has one index-1 preimage K0K^{0}, and q=p−12q=\dfrac{p-1}{2} index-2 preimages K1K^{1}, K2K^{2}, …\dots, KqK^{q}. Denote the corresponding lifts of each 1-cell kik_{i} by ki0k_{i}^{0}, ki1k_{i}^{1}, …\dots, kiqk_{i}^{q}.

There are pp lifts of the 3-cell EE, denoted E0​…​EpE^{0}\dots E^{p}. We again label them by the following rule: Let aa and bb be two points in EE, and g:[0,1]→S3g:[0,1]\rightarrow S^{3} a path from aa to bb which intersects exactly one of the two-cells AiA_{i} once, transversely, where kik_{i} is colored nn. Denote by g~m\tilde{g}_{m} the lift of gg such that g~m​(0)∈Em\tilde{g}_{m}(0)\in E^{m}. Then g~m​(1)∈ERefn​(m)\tilde{g}_{m}(1)\in E^{\text{Ref}_{n}(m)}.

The other cells aia_{i} and AiA_{i} above each have pp lifts to MρM_{\rho}. Let BiB_{i} denote the lift of AiA_{i} incident to ki0k_{i}^{0}. There are two lifts of AiA_{i} incident to each kijk_{i}^{j} for 1≤j≤q1\leq j\leq q, which we denote by RijR_{i}^{j} and LijL_{i}^{j}, labeled as in Section  2. First, arbitrarily label the two lifts of A0A_{0} incident to k0jk_{0}^{j} R0jR_{0}^{j} and L0jL_{0}^{j}. Because the number of crossings of DKD_{K} is even, −∂/∂z-\partial/\partial z has two lifts to MρM_{\rho}. Let VjV^{j} denote the lift of VV tangent to R0jR_{0}^{j}. Then for i≥1i\geq 1, let RijR_{i}^{j} be the lift of AiA_{i} incident to kijk_{i}^{j} and tangent to VjV^{j}, and let LijL_{i}^{j} be the other lift of AiA_{i} incident to kijk_{i}^{j}. Finally, let rijr_{i}^{j} denote the lift of aia_{i} on the boundary of RijR_{i}^{j}, let lijl_{i}^{j} denote the lift of aia_{i} on the boundary of LijL_{i}^{j}, and let bib_{i} be the lift of aia_{i} on the boundary of BiB_{i}. Therefore α00,1=x01−x11−x20,2+1,\alpha_{0}^{0,1}=x_{0}^{1}-x_{1}^{1}-x_{2}^{0,2}+1, which agrees with the direct computation in Section 2.

Theorem 5.

Let q=p−12q=\dfrac{p-1}{2} with pp odd. Let ρ:π1​(S3→K)\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}\rightarrow K) be a pp-coloring of KK, with corresponding irregular pp-fold dihedral cover f:Mρ→S3f:M_{\rho}\rightarrow S^{3}. Let K0K^{0} be the index-1 connected component of f−1​(K)f^{-1}(K) and let K1,K2,…,KqK^{1},K^{2},\dots,K^{q} be the index-2 connected components of f−1​(K)f^{-1}(K). Then KkK^{k} is rationally null-homologous in MρM_{\rho} if and only if the system of equations

xik,j−xi+1k,j−ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−ϵb​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,b⁡(i,j)+Ca​(i,j,k)+Cb​(i,j,k)=0x_{i}^{k,j}-x_{i+1}^{k,j}-\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-\epsilon_{b}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,b(i,j)}+C_{a}(i,j,k)+C_{b}(i,j,k)=0

has a solution (x0k,j,…,xn−1k,j)j=1q∈ℚn​q(x_{0}^{k,j},\dots,x_{n-1}^{k,j})_{j=1}^{q}\in\mathbb{Q}^{nq}.

Furthermore, if k=0k=0, the index-1 lift K0K^{0} of KK bounds the 2-chain

Σ0=∑i=0n−1Bi+∑j=1q∑i=0n−1xi0,j​(Rij−Lij),\Sigma^{0}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}B_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{0,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j}),

and if k≠0k\neq 0, the index-2 lift KkK^{k} of KK bounds the 2-chain

Σk=∑i=0n−1xik,kRik+(1−xik,k)Lik+∑j∈{0,…,q}∖{k}∑i=0n−1xik,j(Rij−Lij).\Sigma^{k}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,k}R_{i}^{k}+(1-x_{i}^{k,k})L_{i}^{k}+\sum_{j\in\{0,\dots,q\}\setminus\{k\}}\quad\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j}).
Proof.

We systematically check each possible configuration of 2-cells incident to rij−lijr_{i}^{j}-l_{i}^{j}, and compute the total number of times rij−lijr_{i}^{j}-l_{i}^{j} appears in the boundary of

Σk=∑i=0n−1xik,kRik+(1−xik,k)Lik+∑j∈{0,…,q}∖{k}∑i=0n−1xik,j(Rij−Lij)\Sigma^{k}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,k}R_{i}^{k}+(1-x_{i}^{k,k})L_{i}^{k}+\sum_{j\in\{0,\dots,q\}\setminus\{k\}}\quad\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j})

if k≠0,k\neq 0,

Σ0=∑i=0n−1Bi+∑j=1q∑i=0n−1xi0,j​(Rij−Lij),\Sigma^{0}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}B_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{0,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j}),

if k=0.k=0.

There are 16 possible configurations. The 8 configurations corresponding to a crossing with positive local writhe number are shown in Figure  9, and the 8 configurations corresponding to a crossing with negative local writhe number are shown in Figure  10. In each case, the coefficients of xik,jx_{i}^{k,j}, xi+1k,jx_{i+1}^{k,j}, xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}, and xo⁡(i)k,b⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,b(i,j)} in αik,j\alpha_{i}^{k,j} are shown, as are the values of ϵa\epsilon_{a} and ϵb\epsilon_{b}. We observe that the coefficients of xik,jx_{i}^{k,j} and xi+1k,jx_{i+1}^{k,j} coming from the boundaries of the “horizontal” 2-cells ∂(xij​(Rij−Lij)+xi+1j​(Ri+1j−Li+1j))\partial(x_{i}^{j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j})+x_{i+1}^{j}(R_{i+1}^{j}-L_{i+1}^{j})) are 1 and -1 respectively. We then check that the coefficients of xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)} and xo⁡(i)k,b⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,b(i,j)} coming from the boundaries of the two “vertical” 2-cells are −ϵa-\epsilon_{a} and −ϵb-\epsilon_{b}, respectively. There are either 0 or 1 additional 2-cells incident to rij−lijr_{i}^{j}-l_{i}^{j}, depending on the value of kk. This contributes the constant term C=Ca+CbC=C_{a}+C_{b} to αik,j\alpha_{i}^{k,j}, where C=0C=0 or ±1\pm 1. If k=0k=0, then C=±1C=\pm 1 if and only if BiB_{i} is incident to rij−lijr_{i}^{j}-l_{i}^{j}. If k≠0k\neq 0, then C=±1C=\pm 1 if and only if a⁡(i,j)=ka(i,j)=k or b⁡(i,j)=kb(i,j)=k. The sign depends on the local writhe number of the crossing. In each of the configurations in Figures  9 and  10, we verify that C=Ca​(i,j,k)+Cb​(i,j,k)C=C_{a}(i,j,k)+C_{b}(i,j,k) is the coefficient of rij−lijr_{i}^{j}-l_{i}^{j} in the relevant additional 2-cell, completing the proof.

5. Computing Linking Numbers

The linking number of KjK^{j} and KkK^{k} is the algebraic intersection number of KjK^{j} with a rational 2-chain bounding KkK^{k}. Theorem  5 determines when such a 2-chain exists and, when it does, describes one such 2-chain Σk\Sigma^{k} explicitly. Now in Theorem  6, we give a formula for the intersection number of KjK^{j} with Σk\Sigma^{k}. By iterating over all j,k∈{0,…,q}j,k\in\{0,\dots,q\}, Theorem  6 allows us to compute the dihedral linking invariant of (K,ρ)(K,\rho). In the statement of the theorem, we allow j=kj=k, in which case the result can be interpreted as a self-linking number of KjK^{j} with respect to a lift of the blackboard framing of the diagram DKD_{K} of KK that determined the cell structure on S3S^{3}.

Theorem 6.

Let q=p−12q=\dfrac{p-1}{2} with pp odd. Let ρ:π1​(S3→K)\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}\rightarrow K) be a pp-coloring of KK, with corresponding irregular pp-fold dihedral cover f:Mρ→S3f:M_{\rho}\rightarrow S^{3}. Suppose that KjK^{j} and KkK^{k}, j,k∈{0,…,q}j,k\in\{0,\dots,q\}, are rationally null-homologous connected components of the singular set f−1​(K)f^{-1}(K). Let Σk\Sigma^{k} be the rational 2-chain given in Theorem  5. Then the linking number of KjK^{j} with KkK^{k} is

lk​(Kj,Kk)=∑i=0n−1Int​(i,j,k)\text{lk}(K^{j},K^{k})=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\text{Int}(i,j,k)

where Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k).\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k).

Note that ϵa​(i,j)=0\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=0 when a⁡(i,j)=0a(i,j)=0, so we treat the first term as 0 in this case even though xik,0x_{i}^{k,0} is not defined.

Proof.

Let (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} be a push-off of KjK^{j}, obtained by pushing KjK^{j} into the 3-cells EhijE^{h_{i}^{j}} such that (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} intersects the 2-skeleton transversely. Let (kij)′(k_{i}^{j})^{\prime} denote the corresponding push-off of kijk_{i}^{j}. Let Int​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k) denote the signed intersection number of (kij)′∪(ki+1j)′¯\overline{(k_{i}^{j})^{\prime}\cup(k_{i+1}^{j})^{\prime}} with Σk\Sigma^{k}.

We now show Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k).

Depending on the values of ϵ⁡(i)\epsilon(i) and ϵa​(i,j)\epsilon_{a}(i,j), (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets one of the 2-cells Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, or Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)} transversely, as shown in Figure  12 when j≠0j\neq 0, and in Figure  14 when j≠0j\neq 0.

Recall that

Σ0=∑i=0n−1Bi+∑j=1q∑i=0n−1xi0,j​(Rij−Lij),\Sigma^{0}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}B_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{0,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j}),

and if k≠0k\neq 0,

Σk=∑i=0n−1xik,kRik+(1−xik,k)Lik+∑j∈{0,…,q}∖{k}∑i=0n−1xik,j(Rij−Lij),\Sigma^{k}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,k}R_{i}^{k}+(1-x_{i}^{k,k})L_{i}^{k}+\sum_{j\in\{0,\dots,q\}\setminus\{k\}}\quad\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}x_{i}^{k,j}(R_{i}^{j}-L_{i}^{j}),

where the xik,jx_{i}^{k,j} are a solution to the system of equations in Theorem  5.

Case 1: k=0k=0.

At crossing ii, (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, or Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)}, as shown in Figure  12 if j≠0j\neq 0 or Figure  14 if j=0j=0.

Case 1a: Suppose (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}. If ϵ⁡(i)=1\epsilon(i)=1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is positive, and the coefficient of Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Then Int​(i,j,k)=xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=1\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=0C_{a}(i,j,k)=0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k) as desired. If instead ϵ⁡(i)=−1\epsilon(i)=-1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is negative, but the coefficient of Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is still xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=−xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. In this case, ϵ⁡(i,j)=−1\epsilon(i,j)=-1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=0C_{a}(i,j,k)=0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k) as well.

Case 1b: Suppose instead that (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}. If ϵ⁡(i)=1\epsilon(i)=1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is positive, and the coefficient of Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is −xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Then Int​(i,j,k)=−xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=−1\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=-1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=0C_{a}(i,j,k)=0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k) as desired. If instead ϵ⁡(i)=−1\epsilon(i)=-1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is negative, but the coefficient of Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is still −xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. In this case, ϵ⁡(i,j)=1\epsilon(i,j)=1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=0C_{a}(i,j,k)=0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k) as well.

Case 1c: Finally, suppose that (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)}. Since k=0k=0, the coefficient of Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is 1. The intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)} is simply Int​(i,j,k)=ϵ​(i)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon(i). In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=0\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=0 and Ca​(i,j,k)=−ϵ⁡(i)C_{a}(i,j,k)=-\epsilon(i). Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k).

Case 2: k≠0k\neq 0.

At crossing ii, (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}, or Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)}, as shown in Figure  12 if j≠0j\neq 0 or Figure  14 if j=0j=0.

Case 2a: Suppose (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Ro⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)R_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)}. This is identical to Case 1a.

Case 2b: Suppose (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} and a⁡(i,j)≠ka(i,j)\neq k. This is identical to Case 1b.

Case 2c: Suppose (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} and a⁡(i,j)=ka(i,j)=k. If ϵ⁡(i)=1\epsilon(i)=1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is positive, and the coefficient of Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is 1−xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)1-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Then Int​(i,j,k)=1−xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=1-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=−1\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=-1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=−1C_{a}(i,j,k)=-1. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k) as desired. If instead ϵ⁡(i)=−1\epsilon(i)=-1, the intersection number of (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} with Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} is negative, but the coefficient of Lo⁡(i)a⁡(i,j)L_{o(i)}^{a(i,j)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is still 1−xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)1-x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−1\text{Int}(i,j,k)=x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-1. In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=1\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=1 and Ca​(i,j,k)=1C_{a}(i,j,k)=1. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k).

Case 2d: Suppose that (Kj)′(K^{j})^{\prime} meets Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)}. Since k≠0k\neq 0, the coefficient of Bo⁡(i)B_{o(i)} in Σk\Sigma^{k} is 0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=0\text{Int}(i,j,k)=0. In this case, ϵa​(i,j)=0\epsilon_{a}(i,j)=0 and Ca​(i,j,k)=0C_{a}(i,j,k)=0. Therefore Int​(i,j,k)=ϵa​(i,j)​xo⁡(i)k,a⁡(i,j)−Ca​(i,j,k)\text{Int}(i,j,k)=\epsilon_{a}(i,j)x_{o(i)}^{k,a(i,j)}-C_{a}(i,j,k).

7. Application: Pseudo-Branch Curves and Computing Ribbon Obstructions

In  [16], Kjuchukova introduced an invariant Ξp​(K,ρ)\Xi_{p}(K,\rho), of a knot KK equipped with a pp-coloring ρ\rho. This invariant gives rise to a homotopy-ribbon obstruction [4, 13], as well as bounds on 4-genera associated to pp-colorable knots [5]. In [6], the first author and Kjuchukova gave a diagrammatic algorithm for computing Ξp\Xi_{p}. This algorithm requires one to compute linking numbers of lifts of curves in S3−KS^{3}-K to the pp-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} along KK; that is, one must compute the linking number of curves other than the branch curves. The first author and Kjuchukova gave an algorithm for computing these linking numbers when p=3p=3 in [7]. In addition, all of the examples of the Ξp\Xi_{p} computation in [6] are carried out for p=3p=3. In the following sections, we give an overview of the linking number computation for a general odd number pp, and then carry out the Ξp\Xi_{p} computation for an example with p>3p>3. This is the first such computation of the Ξp\Xi_{p} invariant. Another explicit method for computing Ξp\Xi_{p} is given in [9], but that method requires additional data—a pp-colorable surface in B4B^{4} over which the pp-coloring of KK extends—and such surfaces need not exist in general [17].

7.1. Computing linking numbers of pseudo-branch curves

The algorithm for computing the linking numbers of the branch curves in a pp-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} along KK extends to an algorithm for computing linking numbers of arbitrary curves in the pp-fold dihedral branched cover, presented as lifts of curves γ\gamma and δ\delta, called pseudo-branch curves, in S3−KS^{3}-K. Such an algorithm was given in the case p=3p=3 by the first author and Kjuchukova in  [7]. Here we give an overview of the algorithm for general odd pp. This algorithm is implemented in the file dihedrallinking_pseudobranch.py at [3] and is used to perform the computation of Ξp\Xi_{p} in the next section.

We begin with a diagram of K∪γ∪δK\cup\gamma\cup\delta. The arcs of the knot KK are equipped with a pp-coloring. Note that the pseudo-branch curves γ\gamma and δ\delta are not colored. In the corresponding map π1​(S3−K∪γ∪δ)↠Dp\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K\cup\gamma\cup\delta)\twoheadrightarrow D_{p}, meridians of γ\gamma and δ\delta map to the identity. Each of γ\gamma and δ\delta has pp path-lifts to the irregular pp-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} branched along KK. For simplicity we will assume that each of these lifts is closed, as is the case in our application. Denote these lifts by γj\gamma^{j} and δk\delta^{k} for j,k∈ℤpj,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. The arcs of the diagram of K∪γ∪δK\cup\gamma\cup\delta are labeled as described in [7]. Briefly, we denote the arcs of γ\gamma by q0,…,qmq_{0},\dots,q_{m} and the arcs of δ\delta by p0,…,pmp_{0},\dots,p_{m}. The lift of qiq_{i} that lies on the lift γj\gamma^{j} is denoted qijq_{i}^{j}. Similarly, pikp_{i}^{k} denotes the lift of pip_{i} that lies on δk.\delta^{k}.

The steps of the algorithm are as follows:

  1. (1)

    Equip S3S^{3} with a cell structure determined by the cone on the link K∪γ∪δK\cup\gamma\cup\delta (presented as a link diagram). This structure consists of “horizontal” 1-cells determined by arcs of KK, γ\gamma, and δ\delta;“vertical” 2-cells below arcs of KK, γ\gamma, and δ\delta; “vertical” 1-cells below all crossings of the diagram; one 3-cell in the complement of the cone; and 0-cells as needed.

  2. (2)

    Lift this cell-structure to the pp-fold irregular dihedral cover of S3S^{3} branched along K.K.

  3. (3)

    Determine the local configuration of the lift of the cell structure in a neighborhood of each crossing. For self-crossings of KK, the lifts are as described in Figures 9 and  10. For positive crossings of KK over or under γ\gamma or δ\delta, the lifts are as described in Figures  16 and  17. One can draw analogous figures for negative crossings.

  4. (4)

    Set up a system of linear equations whose solution determines a 2-chain Σk\Sigma^{k} bounding each rationally null-homologous closed lift δk\delta^{k} of δ\delta. Above crossing ii, the 2-chain will include one copy of the 2-cell incident to po⁡(i)kp_{o(i)}^{k}, as well as some number of copies of each Ril−LilR_{i}^{l}-L_{i}^{l}. The system can be set up by analyzing Figure  16, and the analogous figure for negative crossings.

  5. (5)

    Compute the intersection number of each rationally null-homologous closed lift γj\gamma^{j} of γ\gamma with each 2-chain Σk\Sigma^{k} above. The intersection numbers can be determined by analyzing Figure  17, and the analogous figure for negative crossings. In particular, each arc qijq_{i}^{j} of γj\gamma^{j} terminates at some 2-cell CC; the local intersection number at crossing ii can be computed by multiplying the coefficient of CC in Σk\Sigma^{k} by the sign of crossing ii.

7.2. Computing ribbon obstructions

Let KK be a pp-colored knot in S3S^{3} with Seifert surface Σ\Sigma, and corresponding Seifert matrix VV. A mod pp characteristic knot for KK is an embedded curve β⊂Σ\beta\subset\Sigma such that (V+VT)​β≡0modp(V+V^{T})\beta\equiv 0\mod p [11]. Homology classes of mod pp characteristic knots in H1​(Σ)H_{1}(\Sigma) are in 1-1 correspondence with pp-colorings of KK.

Cappell and Shaneson [11] constructed a cobordism W⁡(K,β)W(K,\beta) from the pp-fold irregular dihedral cover of S3S^{3} along KK, corresponding to a coloring ρ\rho of KK, to the pp-fold cyclic cover of S3S^{3} along a characteristic knot β\beta corresponding to ρ\rho. The following formula for Ξp​(K,ρ)\Xi_{p}(K,\rho) from [16] depends on the signature σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))\sigma(W(K,\beta)) of this cobordism, as well as the Tristram-Levine signatures σζi\sigma_{\zeta_{i}} of β\beta, where the ζi\zeta_{i} denote primitive pthp^{\text{th}} roots of unity, and the self-linking number of β\beta with respect to the symmetrized Seifert form LVL_{V} for Σ\Sigma:

Ξp​(K,ρ)=p2−16​p​LV​(β,β)+∑i=1p−1σζi​(β)+σ⁡(W⁡(K,β)).\Xi_{p}(K,\rho)=\dfrac{p^{2}-1}{6p}L_{V}(\beta,\beta)+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\sigma_{\zeta_{i}}(\beta)+\sigma(W(K,\beta)).

The computation of the first two terms is straightforward. The term σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))\sigma(W(K,\beta)) is equal to the signature of a matrix of linking numbers of certain lifts of a basis for H1​(Σ−β)H_{1}(\Sigma-\beta) to the irregular pp-fold dihedral cover of KK. One can determine which lifts to choose directly from diagrammatic data, as laid out in [6].

We first give an overview of the method of constructing the pp-fold dihedral cover of S3S^{3} along KK from the pp-fold cyclic cover MβM_{\beta} of S3S^{3} along β\beta, and the construction of the cobordism W⁡(K,β)W(K,\beta), from [11]:

  • •

    Let Σ\Sigma be a Seifert surface for KK and β⊂Σ\beta\subset\Sigma a mod pp characteristic knot for KK.

  • •

    Thicken the Seifert surface to obtain Σ×[−1,1]\Sigma\times[-1,1] and let JJ denote its lift to MβM_{\beta}. See Figure  20, top. Note that ∂J\partial J is a union of 2​p2p copies of Σ−β\Sigma-\beta, identified along lifts of the right and left push-offs βr\beta_{r} and βl\beta_{l} of β\beta in Σ\Sigma.

  • •

    Let h:Σ×[−1,1]→Σ×[−1,1]h:\Sigma\times[-1,1]\rightarrow\Sigma\times[-1,1] be the involution mapping x×tx\times t to x×−tx\times-t, and h¯\bar{h} a lift of hh to JJ.

  • •

    The pp-fold irregular dihedral cover of S3S^{3} along KK is homeomorphic to the manifold obtained from M−int​(J)M-\text{int}(J) by identifying points on its boundary ∂J\partial J via h¯\bar{h}. The image of ∂J\partial J under this involution is shown in Figure  20, bottom.

  • •

    The cobordism W⁡(K,β)W(K,\beta) is the mapping cone on h¯\bar{h}, namely Mβ×[0,1]/h¯×1M_{\beta}\times[0,1]/\bar{h}\times 1.

Let {ω1,ω2,…,ωg−1}\{\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\dots,\omega_{g-1}\} denote a basis for H1​(Σ−β)H_{1}(\Sigma-\beta), and let ωi+\omega_{i}^{+} and ωi−\omega_{i}^{-} denote the push-offs of these curves to Σ×1\Sigma\times 1 and Σ×−1\Sigma\times-1 respectively. Each of ωi+\omega_{i}^{+} and ωi−\omega_{i}^{-} has pp lifts to MβM_{\beta}, which lie on ∂J\partial J. The same holds for the push-offs βr±\beta_{r}^{\pm} and βl±\beta_{l}^{\pm}. These lifts bound cylinders in JJ in pairs, and for each curve in {ω1,ω2,…,ωg−1,β}\{\omega_{1},\omega_{2},\dots,\omega_{g-1},\beta\}, (p−1)/2(p-1)/2 of these pairs bound cylinders in h¯​(J)\bar{h}(J). In the schematic diagrams in Figure  20, these pairs lie directly opposite each other on the “spokes” of JJ and h¯​(J)\bar{h}(J) respectively. The corresponding cylinders can be capped off to form closed classes in H2​(W​(K,β))H_{2}(W(K,\beta)) as described in [16, 6]. Therefore the desired signature σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))\sigma(W(K,\beta)) is (after a sign correction) the signature of a matrix MM of linking numbers of these pairs and their push-offs from ∂J\partial J into Mβ−int​(J)M_{\beta}-\text{int}(J); that is, σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))=−σ⁡(M)\sigma(W(K,\beta))=-\sigma(M) [16], [6, Theorem 1].

7.3. Example of Ξp\Xi_{p} computation

We will show that Ξ5​(K)=6\Xi_{5}(K)=6, where KK is the 5-colorable knot in Figure 19. We chose this knot because, in addition to being 5-colorable, it has a diagram in which the characteristic knot β\beta and the basis for H1​(Σ−β)H_{1}(\Sigma-\beta) are relatively simple, but the Seifert surface still has high enough genus to demonstrate the full complexity of the computation. Another reason for choosing this particular knot is that we can confirm the value of Ξp​(K)\Xi_{p}(K) by an alternative method, as follows. The knot KK is the knot K3,5K_{3,5} in the family of knots in Figure 21 of [9]. Section 9 of [9] presents a method for computing Ξp​(K,ρ)\Xi_{p}(K,\rho) using colored tri-plane diagram representations of surfaces in the 4-ball. The method in [9] only applies when one has a pp-colored surface in B4B^{4} with boundary KK over which the coloring ρ\rho extends. This is the case for K3,5K_{3,5}, but there exist other pp-colored knots for which no such surface exists [18]. In contrast, the method presented in [6] and implemented below is fully general.

A Seifert surface for the knot KK, cut along a choice β\beta of characteristic knot, is shown in Figure  19, together with a basis {A,B}\{A,B\} for H1​(Σ−β)H_{1}(\Sigma-\beta). The characteristic knot β\beta is not drawn, but is parallel to its right and left push-offs βr\beta_{r} and βl.\beta_{l}. We pick basepoints on each of KK, AA, BB, βr\beta_{r}, and βl\beta_{l}. These basepoints are marked with dots in Figure  19. Let γr\gamma_{r} and γl\gamma_{l} be paths connecting a basepoint of KK to the basepoints of βr\beta_{r} and βl\beta_{l} respectively, and let γ\gamma be the closed curve on Σ\Sigma obtained by concatenating γr\gamma_{r} and γl\gamma_{l} and identifying their endpoints on βr\beta_{r} and βl\beta_{l}.

We first compute the symmetrized Seifert matrix of KK with respect to the basis {A,B,γ,β}\{A,B,\gamma,\beta\}, from which one can confirm that β\beta is a mod 5 characteristic knot for KK:

[LV]=(2−100−12−100−1−4−1000−100).[L_{V}]=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0&0\\ -1&2&-1&0\\ 0&-1&-4&-10\\ 0&0&-10&0\end{pmatrix}.

In addition, note that the self-linking term LV​(β,β)L_{V}(\beta,\beta) of Ξ5​(K)\Xi_{5}(K) is equal to zero.

We equip S3S^{3} with the cell structure determined by the cone on K=K3,5K=K_{3,5} as described in Section  3.

For each curve C∈{A,B,β,βr,βl}C\in\{A,B,\beta,\beta_{r},\beta_{l}\}, let C+C^{+} denote the push-off of CC to Σ×1\Sigma\times 1 and let C−C^{-} denote the push-off of CC to Σ×−1\Sigma\times-1. For i∈{0,…,4}i\in\{0,\dots,4\}, let CiC^{i}, Ci,+C^{i,+}, and Ci,−C^{i,-} denote the lifts of CC, C+C^{+}, and C−C^{-} such that the lift of the basepoint lies in the 3-cell Ei.E^{i}. Now let C∈{A,B,βr}C\in\{A,B,\beta_{r}\}. We choose paths δA,δB\delta_{A},\delta_{B} and γr\gamma_{r} (called anchor paths in [6]) connecting the basepoint of each CC to the basepoint of KK; for simplicity we choose these paths such that their interiors are disjoint from KK. To determine which pairs Ci,+C^{i,+} and Cj,−C^{j,-} bound cylinders in JJ, observe that traveling from the basepoint of C+C^{+} to the basepoint of K+K^{+} along a positive push-off of δA\delta_{A}, δB\delta_{B}, or γr\gamma_{r}, and then to the basepoint of C−C^{-} along the negative push-off of δA\delta_{A}, δB\delta_{B}, or γr\gamma_{r}, requires passing through the vertical 2-cell below the basepoint of KK one time. If KK is colored cc, this means one will pass from the 3-cell EiE^{i} to the 3-cell ERefc​(i)E^{\text{Ref}_{c}(i)}, where j=Refc​(i)j=\text{Ref}_{c}(i) if vertices jj and ii of the regular pp-gon are related by reflection over the line through vertex cc. Therefore for C∈{A,B,βr}C\in\{A,B,\beta_{r}\}, Ci,+C^{i,+} and CRefc​(i),−C^{\text{Ref}_{c}(i),-} bound a cylinder in J.J. See Figure  18. The superscripts of the lifts of βl\beta_{l} can be determined by the monodromy associated to the anchor path γl\gamma_{l}, as discussed in [6]; this information can be used to determine the superscripts of all lifts of positive and negative push-offs of {A,B,β,βr,βl}\{A,B,\beta,\beta_{r},\beta_{l}\} as shown in Figure 20.

For our 5-colored diagram of K=K3,5K=K_{3,5}, note that the basepoint of KK lies on an arc colored 1. When the vertices of a regular 5-gon are labeled 0,…,4 in counter-clockwise order, the vertices 0 and 2 are related by reflection over the line through 1, as are the vertices 3 and 4. Therefore for C∈{A,B,βr}C\in\{A,B,\beta_{r}\}, C0,+C^{0,+} and C2,−C^{2,-} bound a cylinder in JJ, as do C3,+C^{3,+} and C4,−C^{4,-}. After applying the involution h¯\bar{h}, Ci,±C^{i,\pm} is identified with Ci,∓C^{i,\mp}. Therefore C0C^{0} and C2C^{2} bound a cylinder in h¯​(J)\bar{h}(J), as do C3C^{3} and C4C^{4}.

Recall that σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))=−σ⁡(M)\sigma(W(K,\beta))=-\sigma(M), where MM is a matrix of linking numbers of curves that bound cylinders in h¯​(J)\bar{h}(J). In this case, MM is a 6×66\times 6 matrix, whose entries are, for each C∈{A,B,β}C\in\{A,B,\beta\}, linking numbers of C0−C2C^{0}-C^{2} and C3−C4C^{3}-C^{4} with their push-offs into the interior of Mβ−int​(J)M_{\beta}-\text{int}(J), namely C0,+−C2,−C^{0,+}-C^{2,-} and C3,+−C4,−C^{3,+}-C^{4,-}. (In order to land in the interior of Mβ−int​(J)M_{\beta}-\text{int}(J), we assume these push-offs lie on lifts of Σ×±(1+ϵ)\Sigma\times\pm(1+\epsilon).)

We begin by applying the algorithm in Section 7.1 to compute the linking numbers of all lifts of A,BA,B, and β\beta with all lifts of each of their positive push-offs with respect to Σ\Sigma. These linking numbers are computed in the file Xi_computation.ipynb at [3], and are displayed in Table  1.

We use the linking numbers in Table  1 to determine the matrix MM, which is shown in Table  2. All eigenvalues of this matrix MM are negative. Therefore σ⁡(M)=−6\sigma(M)=-6, and σ⁡(W⁡(K,β))=6.\sigma(W(K,\beta))=6.

Finally we compute Ξ5​(K3,5)\Xi_{5}(K_{3,5}) using the formula in Section 7.2. As the characteristic knot is an unknot, its Tristram-Levine signatures vanish. In addition, the self-linking number LV​(β,β)L_{V}(\beta,\beta) is zero. Hence Ξ5​(K3,5)=6\Xi_{5}(K_{3,5})=6. This agrees with the value computed in [9] using trisections.

In [5], the first author and Kjuchukova introduced the notion of the pp-dihedral genus 𝔤p​(K,ρ)\mathfrak{g}_{p}(K,\rho) of a knot KK with respect to a pp-coloring ρ\rho, which is the minimum genus of a locally flat, orientable surface in B4B^{4} over which the coloring ρ\rho extends. In Theorem 1 of [5], we proved

𝔤p​(K,ρ)≥|Ξp​(K,ρ)|−rk ​H1​(Mρ,ℤ)p−1−12.\mathfrak{g}_{p}(K,\rho)\geq\dfrac{|\Xi_{p}(K,\rho)|-\text{rk }H_{1}(M_{\rho};\mathbb{Z})}{p-1}-\dfrac{1}{2}.

The knot KK above is 2-bridge, from which it follows that 1) the coloring ρ\rho in Figure 19 is the unique 5-coloring of KK up to equivalence, and 2) the corresponding 5-fold dihedral cover MρM_{\rho} is homeomorphic to S3S^{3}. Substituting Ξ5​(K,ρ)=6\Xi_{5}(K,\rho)=6 into this bound, we conclude 𝔤5​(K,ρ)≥1.\mathfrak{g}_{5}(K,\rho)\geq 1. Furthermore, as KK has a unique 5-coloring, if KK were homotopy-ribbon, ρ\rho would have to extend over any choice of homotopy-ribbon disk for KK [4, 13]. As 𝔤p​(K,ρ)≥1\mathfrak{g}_{p}(K,\rho)\geq 1, we conclude KK is not homotopy-ribbon. Observe from the symmetrized Seifert form LVL_{V} above that the Murasugi signature σ⁡(K)\sigma(K) is equal to 2, so we can also conclude that the topological 4-genus of KK is at least 1 via other methods. A necessary condition for the topological 4-genus and dihedral 4-genus to coincide was given in Theorem 1 of [5]. A more thorough comparison of these genera is a worthy topic for further study.

8. Tabulation of the Dihedral Linking Invariant

Throughout this section all data on knot polynomials is obtained from Knot Info [20]. All data on mutants, specifically the tabulation of groups of mutant knots through 13 crossings, is due to Stoimenov [27]. Our computations and tabulations are available at [3].

8.1. Tabulation

Let KK be a knot with det​(K)≠1\text{det}(K)\neq 1 and pp a prime dividing det​(K)\text{det}(K). Let Σ2​(K)\Sigma_{2}(K) denote the double branched cover of S3S^{3} along KK. Each pp-coloring of KK corresponds to a nontrivial homomorphism H1​(Σ2​(K),ℤ)↠ℤpH_{1}(\Sigma_{2}(K);\mathbb{Z})\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{p}. We call two such homomorphisms equivalent if they are related by multiplication by a unit in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}. Let CpC_{p} denote the set of equivalence classes of pp-colorings of KK. We define the number of pp-colorings of KK to be the number of equivalence classes of such homomorphisms |Cp||C_{p}|. Observe that |Cp|=pn−1p−1|C_{p}|=\dfrac{p^{n}-1}{p-1}, where nn is the number of pkp^{k}-cyclic summands in the elementary divisor decomposition of H1​(Σ2​(K),ℤ)H_{1}(\Sigma_{2}(K);\mathbb{Z}).

Recall that given a pp-coloring ρ:π1​(S3−K)↠ℤp\rho:\pi_{1}(S^{3}-K)\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{p} we define the corresponding dihedral linking invariant to be

D​L​N​(K,ρ)={lk​(Ki,Kj)|i≠j∈{0,1,…,(p−1)/2}}.DLN(K,\rho)=\left\{\text{lk}(K^{i},K^{j})|i\neq j\in\{0,1,\dots,(p-1)/2\}\right\}.

The linking numbers between the various index-2 curves can be recovered from linking numbers with the index-1 curve K0K^{0} (see [11, p. 168], remark above Theorem II). Therefore it suffices to study

D​L​N0​(K,ρ)={lk​(K0,Kj)|j∈{0,1,…,(p−1)/2}}.DLN_{0}(K,\rho)=\left\{\text{lk}(K^{0},K^{j})|j\in\{0,1,\dots,(p-1)/2\}\right\}.

Next we define the total dihedral linking invariant of KK to be

D​L​N​(K)=⋃p≥3​ prime ⋃[ρ]∈Cp{(p,D​L​N0​(K,ρ))}.DLN(K)=\bigcup_{p\geq 3\text{ prime }}\bigcup_{[\rho]\in C_{p}}\{(p,DLN_{0}(K,\rho))\}.

Our tabulation of D​L​N​(K)DLN(K) for prime knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 is available in the file data/tabulation_with_colorings.csv at [3]. To carry out the tabulation of D​L​NDLN, we extract a list of knots, their braid words, and determinants from Knot Info [20]. For each prime pp with 3≤p≤det​(K)3\leq p\leq\text{det}(K), we check whether pp divides the determinant det​(K)\text{det}(K) of KK. If so, we solve a system of linear equations (determined from the braid word) mod pp to determine all pp-colorings of KK, and then choose one representative of each equivalence class of the set of all pp-colorings of KK. We then run dihedrallinking.py to compute the values of D​L​N0​(K,ρ)DLN_{0}(K,\rho) for each pp-coloring ρ\rho, extracting the overstrand and sign lists from the braid word. The tabulation of the linking invariant for 3-colorable knots up to 11 crossings is due to Perko  [22].

We note that the D​L​N​(K)DLN(K) invariant can take on pn−1p−1\dfrac{p^{n}-1}{p-1} distinct values on the pn−1p−1\dfrac{p^{n}-1}{p-1} equivalence classes of pp-colorings of KK. For p=3p=3 and n=2n=2, i.e., knots with four equivalence classes of 3-colorings, there are exactly 57 prime knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 whose four 3-dihedral linking invariants (each of which is a single element of ℚ∪{∞}\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}) are distinct. The first such knot in the tables is 12_n388, whose four linking numbers are 0, 2, 4, and 6.

For p=5p=5 and n=2n=2, i.e., knots with six equivalence classes of 5-colorings, there is just one prime knot of crossing number ≤13\leq 13, namely 13a_3773, whose six 5-dihedral linking invariants (each of which is a two-element subset of ℚ∪{∞}\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}) are distinct. These six values of the 5-dihedral linking invariant of 13a_3773 are:

{−54/5,86/5},{−34/5,66/5},{−24/5,16/5},{−14/5,46/5},{−4/5,−4/5},{6/55,166/55}.\{-54/5,86/5\},\{-34/5,66/5\},\{-24/5,16/5\},\{-14/5,46/5\},\{-4/5,-4/5\},\{6/55,166/55\}.

Through 13 crossings, there are five additional prime knots such that five of the six 5-dihedral linking invariants are distinct: 13n_1026, 13n_1102, 13n_4173, 13a_3581, and 13a_3760.

For p=7p=7 and n=2n=2, i.e., knots with eight equivalence classes of 7-colorings, there are no prime knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 whose eight 7-dihedral linking invariants (each of which is a three-element subset of ℚ∪{∞}\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}) are all distinct. There are three knots with eight distinct 7-colorings through 13 crossings that have seven distinct 7-dihedral linking invariants: 13a_1067, 13a_2330, 13n_2694.

8.2. Comparing the total dihedral linking invariant to other invariants

The coloring invariant col​(K)\text{col}(K) of KK is the set of pairs (p,|Cp|)(p,|C_{p}|), where pp is a prime dividing det​(K)\text{det}(K) and |Cp||C_{p}| is the number of pp-colorings of KK. We first focus on distinguishing knots with the same coloring invariant, since we include the data of the coloring invariant in the total dihedral linking invariant.

Through 13 crossings, there are 673,562 pairs of knots with the same coloring invariant. The total dihedral linking invariant distinguishes 663,344, or 98.48%, of those pairs.

We now compare the dihedral linking invariant to various polynomial invariants. Table 3 demonstrates the ability of the dihedral linking invariant to distinguish knots that have the same coloring invariant, and the same Alexander, Jones, HOMFLY-PT, Kauffman, or unreduced Khovanov ℤ\mathbb{Z}-polynomial.

Upon further investigation, many of the above pairs that the dihedral linking invariant does not distinguish are in fact mutants. Therefore, we also test the ability of the dihedral linking invariant to distinguish non-mutant knots with the same coloring invariant and polynomial invariant. The results of this experiment are shown in Table 4. The dihedral invariant is remarkably strong in this context, distinguishing between 94% and 98% of such pairs, depending on the polynomial chosen.

While we have not found any mutant pairs distinguished by the dihedral linking invariant up to crossing number 13, we do not know whether the dihedral linking invariant is mutation-invariant in general. Perko has shown that linking invariants in other branched covers can distinguish mutants [24].

In Table 5, we list the 20 pairs of non-mutant knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 that have the same HOMFLY-PT polynomial and the same dihedral linking invariant (and hence the same coloring invariant). Similarly, there are three pairs of knots of crossing number ≤13\leq 13 that have the same Kauffman polynomial and the same dihedral linking invariant, and are not mutants: 12a_325 and 12a_711; 12a_390 and 12a_672; and 13a_1312 and 13a_1592. These three pairs also have the same HOMFLY-PT polynomial, and so also appear in Table 5.

We display selected pairs of knots with the same HOMFLY-PT polynomial and coloring invariant that are distinguished by the dihedral linking invariant in Tables 6 and 7. Namely, we display data for knots with crossing number ≤12\leq 12 such that the largest prime dividing det​(K)\text{det}(K) is 7. We do the same for the Kauffman polynomial in Table 8.
